specStatements.text: Students should be able to describe cellular respiration as an exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells.
The energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes.
Respiration in cells can take place aerobically (using oxygen) or anaerobically (without oxygen), to transfer energy.
Students should be able to compare the processes of aerobic and anaerobic respiration with regard to the need for oxygen, the differing products and the relative amounts of energy transferred.
Organisms need energy for: chemical reactions to build larger molecules; movement; keeping warm.
Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation:
glucose +oxygen → carbon dioxide +water
Students should recognise the chemical symbols: C6 H12 O6 , O2 , CO2 and H2 O.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation:
glucose →lactic acid
As the oxidation of glucose is incomplete in anaerobic respiration much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by the equation:
glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells is called fermentation and has economic importance in the manufacture of bread and alcoholic drinks.
During exercise the human body reacts to the increased demand for energy.
The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.

If insufficient oxygen is supplied anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles. The incomplete oxidation of glucose causes a build up of lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt. During long periods of vigorous activity muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently.

Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
Students should be able to explain the importance of sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol in the synthesis and breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.
Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body.
The energy transferred by respiration in cells is used by the organism for the continual enzyme controlled processes of metabolism that synthesise new molecules.

Metabolism includes: conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins; respiration; breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion.
All of these aspects are covered in more detail in the relevant specification section but are linked together here.

scopeNotes.statement: All of these aspects are covered in more detail in the relevant specification section but are linked together here.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The metabolism items stay at the level of the linked list given in 4.4.2.3. Glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose, lipid formation from glycerol and fatty acids, glucose and nitrate ions forming amino acids, respiration, and the breakdown of excess proteins to form urea are each treated as named parts of metabolism. The detail that belongs to other specification sections, such as the chemistry of enzyme action, the mechanism of digestion and absorption, the structure of the liver or the excretion of urea by the kidney, is not developed here.

concepts.definition: An exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells, transferring energy from glucose. The energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes.
A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings. Because respiration is exothermic, respiring cells and tissues get warmer as energy is transferred.

concepts.term: Uses of the energy transferred by respiration
concepts.definition: Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for movement, and for keeping warm. The energy transferred is also used for the continual enzyme controlled processes of metabolism that synthesise new molecules.
Respiration in cells that takes place using oxygen. Glucose is completely oxidised, so a relatively large amount of energy is transferred compared with anaerobic respiration.
Respiration in cells that takes place without oxygen, to transfer energy. The products differ from those of aerobic respiration and much less energy is transferred.
Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water. These symbols are used in place of the words in the equation for aerobic respiration.
Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation: glucose → lactic acid. No carbon dioxide or water is produced by this reaction.
In anaerobic respiration the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.

concepts.term: Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells
concepts.definition: Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by the equation: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.

Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells. It has economic importance in the manufacture of bread, where the carbon dioxide makes the dough rise, and of alcoholic drinks, which contain the ethanol produced.

concepts.term: Response of the body to exercise
concepts.definition: During exercise the human body reacts to the increased demand for energy. The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.

concepts.term: Muscle fatigue and oxygen debt in exercise
concepts.definition: If insufficient oxygen is supplied, anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles. The incomplete oxidation of glucose causes a build up of lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt. During long periods of vigorous activity muscles become fatigued and stop contracting efficiently.

concepts.term: Oxygen debt and the fate of lactic acid
concepts.definition: Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

The sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body. The energy transferred by respiration in cells is used by the organism for these continual enzyme controlled processes, which synthesise new molecules.

Metabolism includes: conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins; respiration; and the breakdown of excess proteins to form urea for excretion.

concepts.term: Small molecules used in synthesis and breakdown
concepts.definition: Sugars are used to synthesise carbohydrates such as starch, glycogen and cellulose; amino acids are used to synthesise proteins, and excess protein is broken down to form urea; glycerol and fatty acids are used to synthesise lipids. Breakdown of these larger molecules releases the same small molecules again.

misconceptions.question: Is respiration the same thing as breathing?
misconceptions.correct: Respiration is an exothermic reaction occurring continuously in living cells that transfers energy from glucose. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs, and the breathing rate increases during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
misconceptions.misconception: Respiration is breathing air in and out, so it happens in the lungs rather than in cells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'respiration' and 'respiratory system' are used for breathing, and both processes involve oxygen and carbon dioxide, so students merge the two.
misconceptions.correction: Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells. Breathing supplies the oxygen used in aerobic respiration and removes the carbon dioxide made, but it is not respiration itself.

misconceptions.question: When do cells respire?
misconceptions.correct: Respiration occurs continuously in living cells, whether the organism is resting or exercising.
misconceptions.misconception: Cells only respire when the body is exercising and needs extra energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Respiration is usually met through examples about exercise and muscles, so students link it to activity rather than to all living cells all of the time.
misconceptions.correction: Cellular respiration is continuously occurring in living cells because the energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes, including at rest.

misconceptions.question: Is respiration exothermic or endothermic?
misconceptions.correct: Respiration is an exothermic reaction, so it transfers energy to the surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: Respiration is endothermic because the cell has to take in energy to make the reaction happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see that glucose and oxygen are taken into the cell and assume energy must be taken in as well, and 'exothermic' and 'endothermic' are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction, which is why organisms can use the energy transferred for keeping warm.

misconceptions.question: Does respiration make energy for the cell?
misconceptions.correct: Respiration transfers energy from glucose; the energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes.
misconceptions.misconception: Respiration creates new energy inside the cell, and that energy is then used up and destroyed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Phrases such as 'releases energy' and 'produces energy' are common in everyday language, so energy is treated as a substance that can be made and destroyed.
misconceptions.correction: Energy is transferred, not made. The energy transferred by respiration supplies all the energy needed for living processes such as building larger molecules, movement and keeping warm.

misconceptions.question: What is the energy transferred by respiration used for in chemical reactions?
misconceptions.correct: It is used for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for example forming starch, glycogen, lipids and proteins.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy from respiration is used to break large molecules down into small ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate respiration with the breakdown of glucose and assume that other reactions in the body must also be breakdown reactions.
misconceptions.correction: Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, as well as for movement and keeping warm. Metabolism uses this energy in enzyme controlled processes that synthesise new molecules.

misconceptions.question: What are the reactants of aerobic respiration?
misconceptions.correct: The reactants are glucose and oxygen; the products are carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.misconception: Aerobic respiration uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Respiration and photosynthesis are taught as linked processes with the same four substances, so students reverse the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, so glucose and oxygen are used up and carbon dioxide and water are produced.

misconceptions.question: Which substance does the symbol C6H12O6 represent?
misconceptions.correct: C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water.
misconceptions.misconception: When reading the respiration symbols, students match a formula to a substance by the letters it contains rather than reading the whole formula, so any formula that contains an O is taken to be oxygen and the different symbols get muddled up with one another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match symbols by the letters they can see rather than reading the whole formula, and both formulae contain C and O.
misconceptions.correction: Students should recognise the chemical symbols: C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water.

misconceptions.question: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in muscle cells?
misconceptions.correct: Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation glucose → lactic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces carbon dioxide and water, the same as aerobic respiration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The aerobic equation is learned first and students apply its products to every kind of respiration, especially as people do breathe out carbon dioxide during exercise.
misconceptions.correction: Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation glucose → lactic acid. The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so carbon dioxide and water are not the products.

misconceptions.question: What is produced by anaerobic respiration in yeast cells?
misconceptions.correct: Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by the equation glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Anaerobic respiration makes the same products in every kind of cell, so lactic acid and ethanol are treated as interchangeable and either one can be given as the product for muscle cells or for yeast cells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lactic acid is met first, in the well known example of muscles during exercise, and is then treated as the product of all anaerobic respiration.
misconceptions.correction: Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid, but anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

misconceptions.question: Which transfers more energy from each glucose molecule, aerobic or anaerobic respiration?
misconceptions.correct: Aerobic respiration transfers much more energy, because the oxidation of glucose in anaerobic respiration is incomplete.
misconceptions.misconception: Anaerobic respiration transfers more energy because it happens faster and is used for sprinting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Anaerobic respiration is associated with sudden bursts of intense activity, so students confuse the rate of the reaction with the amount of energy transferred per glucose molecule.
misconceptions.correction: As the oxidation of glucose is incomplete in anaerobic respiration, much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.

misconceptions.question: Does fermentation in yeast need oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast cells, so it takes place without oxygen.
misconceptions.misconception: Fermentation still needs a small amount of oxygen, because all living cells need oxygen to respire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that organisms need oxygen to survive and assume no cell can transfer energy without it, so they add oxygen to the fermentation equation.
misconceptions.correction: Respiration can take place anaerobically, without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells is called fermentation and is represented by glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, with no oxygen used.

misconceptions.question: What changes in the body during exercise?
misconceptions.correct: The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume all increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
misconceptions.misconception: During exercise you only breathe faster; the volume of each breath and the heart rate stay the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Faster breathing is the change students notice in themselves, while breath volume cannot be felt directly and the heart rate is only noticed if it is measured.
misconceptions.correction: The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.

misconceptions.question: Where is the lactic acid made during exercise converted back into glucose?
misconceptions.correct: Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.
misconceptions.misconception: Lactic acid is dealt with where it is made, so it is broken down inside the muscles or in the blood itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lactic acid builds up in muscles and that is where the aching is felt, so students assume the muscle also removes it and do not connect the process with another organ.
misconceptions.correction: Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.

misconceptions.question: How is a lipid molecule formed?
misconceptions.correct: A lipid molecule is formed from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.
misconceptions.misconception: A lipid is formed from three molecules of glycerol joined to one molecule of fatty acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the numbers one and three are involved but not which small molecule each number belongs to, and 'glycerol' and 'fatty acid' are unfamiliar names.
misconceptions.correction: Metabolism includes the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.

misconceptions.question: What does a plant need in order to make amino acids?
misconceptions.correct: Glucose and nitrate ions are used to form amino acids, which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.
misconceptions.misconception: Amino acids can be made from glucose on its own, without nitrate ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Glucose is remembered as the starting point for everything a plant makes, and the nitrate ions taken up by the roots are easy to leave out because they are not part of photosynthesis.
misconceptions.correction: Metabolism includes the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.

misconceptions.question: Can any small molecule be used to build any larger molecule?
misconceptions.correct: Each larger molecule is built from its own small molecules: sugars build carbohydrates, glycerol and fatty acids build lipids, and amino acids build proteins.
misconceptions.misconception: The small molecules are interchangeable, so amino acids, glycerol or sugars can be used to build whichever larger molecule the cell needs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The small molecules are all products of digestion that are met together in one list, so students treat them as one general supply of building blocks.
misconceptions.correction: Metabolism includes conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; and the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.

options.text: an endothermic reaction happening in all living cells
options.rationale: A student who thinks the cell must take energy in to break glucose down chooses endothermic. Respiration is exothermic: it transfers energy to the surroundings, which is how organisms keep warm.

options.text: an exothermic reaction happening during exercise
options.rationale: A student who links respiration only to periods of activity picks this. Respiration is continuously occurring in living cells, at rest as well as during exercise.

options.text: an exothermic reaction occurring continuously in living cells
options.rationale: Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells, transferring the energy needed for living processes.

options.text: an exothermic reaction happening when we breathe in
options.rationale: A student who treats respiration as breathing places it in the lungs. Breathing supplies oxygen for respiration, but the reaction itself takes place in living cells.

mcqs.stem: How does anaerobic respiration in muscle cells compare with aerobic respiration?

options.text: far more energy transferred, and lactic acid made
options.rationale: A student who thinks the faster process must transfer more energy picks this. The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.

options.text: less energy transferred, and lactic acid made
options.rationale: Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by glucose → lactic acid, and because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.

options.text: less energy transferred, and ethanol also made
options.rationale: A student who applies one set of anaerobic products to every cell picks ethanol. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are made in plant and yeast cells; muscle cells make lactic acid.

options.text: less energy transferred, and carbon dioxide made
options.rationale: A student who carries the aerobic products across to anaerobic respiration picks carbon dioxide. In muscles the equation is glucose → lactic acid, with no carbon dioxide produced.

mcqs.stem: Which is a use of the energy transferred by respiration?

options.text: creating new energy inside the cell
options.rationale: A student who treats energy as something the cell manufactures picks this. Respiration transfers energy from glucose; it does not create energy.

options.text: moving oxygen out of the lungs and into the blood
options.rationale: A student who confuses respiration with breathing picks a gas exchange step. Oxygen moves into the blood by diffusion; the energy transferred by respiration is used for building molecules, movement and keeping warm.

options.text: building larger molecules from smaller ones
options.rationale: Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, as well as for movement and keeping warm.

options.text: breaking large molecules down into smaller ones
options.rationale: A student who thinks energy is needed for breakdown reactions picks this. The specification states that organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation represents aerobic respiration?

options.text: glucose → carbon dioxide + water
options.rationale: A student who thinks respiration makes carbon dioxide and water whether or not oxygen is present drops the oxygen from the equation. Aerobic respiration needs oxygen as a reactant: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

options.text: carbon dioxide + water → sugars + oxygen
options.rationale: A student who remembers that respiration and photosynthesis involve the same substances reverses the equation. In aerobic respiration glucose and oxygen are the reactants.

options.text: glucose + oxygen → ethanol + carbon dioxide
options.rationale: A student who thinks fermentation needs oxygen writes oxygen into it. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products of anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells, which uses no oxygen.

options.text: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
options.rationale: This is the equation given in the specification for aerobic respiration: glucose and oxygen are used and carbon dioxide and water are produced.

mcqs.stem: In the equation for aerobic respiration, what do the symbols C6H12O6 and H2O represent?

options.text: C6H12O6 is glucose and H2O is oxygen
options.rationale: A student who reads only the O in the formula calls it oxygen. Oxygen is O2; H2O is water.

options.text: C6H12O6 is oxygen gas and H2O is water
options.rationale: A student matching letters rather than whole formulae sees the O in C6H12O6 and calls it oxygen. Oxygen is O2 and C6H12O6 is glucose.

options.text: C6H12O6 is water and H2O is glucose
options.rationale: A student who has learned the symbols as a list without linking them to substances swaps them over. C6H12O6 is glucose and H2O is water.

options.text: C6H12O6 is glucose and H2O is the water produced
options.rationale: C6H12O6 is the symbol for glucose, the reactant, and H2O is the symbol for water, one of the products.

mcqs.stem: A muscle cell has no oxygen supply. Which substance builds up in the cell?

options.text: liquid ethanol, made from glucose
options.rationale: A student who uses one equation for all anaerobic respiration picks ethanol. Ethanol is made in plant and yeast cells, not in muscles.

options.text: lactic acid, made from glucose
options.rationale: Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation glucose → lactic acid, so lactic acid builds up when insufficient oxygen is supplied.

options.text: water vapour, made from glucose
options.rationale: A student who applies the aerobic products to anaerobic respiration picks water. Water is a product of aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.

options.text: carbon dioxide gas, made from glucose
options.rationale: A student who assumes every kind of respiration releases carbon dioxide picks this. In muscles the only product of anaerobic respiration is lactic acid.

mcqs.stem: Why is much less energy transferred by anaerobic respiration than by aerobic respiration?

options.text: the oxidation of glucose is faster
options.rationale: A student who confuses the speed of the reaction with the energy transferred picks this. The amount of energy transferred is lower because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete.

options.text: the glucose stored in cells is used up faster
options.rationale: A student who reasons that a fast reaction must run out of fuel picks this. The reason given in the specification is the incomplete oxidation of glucose.

options.text: the energy is used up making lactic acid
options.rationale: A student who treats energy as a substance that gets consumed and destroyed picks this. Less energy is transferred because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete.

options.text: the oxidation of glucose is incomplete
options.rationale: As the oxidation of glucose is incomplete in anaerobic respiration, much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.

mcqs.stem: Yeast is used in the manufacture of bread and alcoholic drinks. Which equation represents the respiration of the yeast in these processes?

options.text: glucose → lactic acid
options.rationale: A student who thinks all anaerobic respiration makes lactic acid picks this. Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

options.text: glucose + oxygen → ethanol + carbon dioxide
options.rationale: A student who believes fermentation still needs some oxygen picks this. Fermentation is anaerobic respiration, so it takes place without oxygen and the other product is carbon dioxide.

options.text: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide
options.rationale: Anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells is represented by this equation. In yeast it is called fermentation: the carbon dioxide makes bread rise and the ethanol is in alcoholic drinks.

options.text: glucose → ethanol + oxygen
options.rationale: A student who confuses respiration with photosynthesis writes oxygen as a product. Fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide, and no oxygen is involved.

mcqs.stem: How does the body react to the increased demand for energy during exercise?

options.text: heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume rise
options.rationale: The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.

options.text: the breathing rate rises but the heart rate stays steady
options.rationale: A student who notices only their own faster breathing picks this. The heart rate also increases, to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.

options.text: the breathing rate rises but the breath volume stays the same
options.rationale: A student who thinks only the rate of breathing changes picks this. The volume of each breath deepens as well, so breath volume increases alongside the breathing rate.

options.text: the breath volume rises but the heart rate is unchanged
options.rationale: A student who treats respiration as a lung process expects only breathing to change. The heart rate increases too, because the blood transports the oxygen to the muscles.

mcqs.stem: A sprinter's muscles are not supplied with enough oxygen during a race. What happens in the muscles?

options.text: lactic acid builds up and an oxygen debt forms
options.rationale: If insufficient oxygen is supplied, anaerobic respiration takes place in muscles; the incomplete oxidation of glucose causes a build up of lactic acid and creates an oxygen debt.

options.text: carbon dioxide builds up and an oxygen debt forms
options.rationale: A student who uses the aerobic products for anaerobic respiration picks carbon dioxide. Anaerobic respiration in muscles is glucose → lactic acid.

options.text: ethanol builds up and an oxygen debt is created
options.rationale: A student who applies the yeast equation to muscle picks ethanol. Ethanol and carbon dioxide are produced by plant and yeast cells, not by muscles.

options.text: lactic acid builds up and more energy is transferred
options.rationale: A student who thinks anaerobic respiration is the higher energy process picks this. Because the oxidation of glucose is incomplete, much less energy is transferred.

mcqs.stem: After a race, what happens to the lactic acid that has built up in the muscles?

options.text: it is taken in the blood to the liver
options.rationale: Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose.

options.text: it is broken down inside the muscles
options.rationale: A student who assumes lactic acid is dealt with where it is made picks this. Blood flowing through the muscles transports it to the liver.

options.text: it is breathed out through the lungs as vapour
options.rationale: A student who confuses respiration with breathing expects the waste to leave in exhaled air. The extra oxygen taken in after exercise is used to react with the lactic acid, which is carried to the liver.

options.text: it is turned back into glucose in the blood
options.rationale: A student who knows lactic acid becomes glucose again but not where picks the blood. The blood transports it; the conversion happens in the liver.

mcqs.stem: How is a lipid molecule formed in metabolism?

options.text: from three glycerols and a fatty acid
options.rationale: A student who remembers the numbers but not which molecule they belong to reverses them. One glycerol joins to three fatty acids.

options.text: from a single glycerol and three amino acids
options.rationale: A student who treats the small molecules as interchangeable puts amino acids into a lipid. Amino acids are used to synthesise proteins; lipids are made from glycerol and fatty acids.

options.text: from three fatty acids and one glucose
options.rationale: A student who uses glucose as the starting point for everything picks this. Glucose is converted to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the lipid partner of fatty acids is glycerol.

options.text: from one glycerol and three fatty acids
options.rationale: Metabolism includes the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.

mcqs.stem: A plant cell synthesises protein. Which molecules does its metabolism use?

options.text: glucose and some fatty acids, to make amino acids
options.rationale: A student who leaves out the nitrate ions picks another organic molecule instead. Nitrate ions are needed with glucose to form amino acids.

options.text: glucose and nitrate ions, used to make amino acids
options.rationale: Metabolism includes the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.

options.text: glycerol and nitrate ions, to make amino acids
options.rationale: A student who treats the small molecules as interchangeable substitutes glycerol for glucose. Glycerol is used with fatty acids to form lipids.

options.text: starch and nitrate ions, to make amino acids
options.rationale: A student who does not distinguish between the sugar and the storage carbohydrate picks starch. Glucose is converted to starch for storage; it is glucose that is used with nitrate ions.
